images.description: Diagram of two application instances each holding a private in-memory cache of the same SQL database, with callouts explaining that instance A caches a snapshot at time X, instance B caches at time Y, and the database changes in between, so the two caches diverge.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of a shared cache service sitting between a SQL database and two application instances, with a callout noting that both application instances see the same cached data.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram combining a shared cache service with local private caches in application instances A and B, with callouts explaining that if the shared cache service is unavailable, instances keep functioning using local private caches populated from the database.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram comparing content delivery latency: clients reach the origin server directly in 120ms versus fetching the same image from a nearby CDN edge node in 40ms, with the CDN pulling content from the origin.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of horizontal partitioning (sharding): a product table is split by key range into an A-G shard and an H-Z shard, with each shard holding complete rows for its key range.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of vertical partitioning: a single product table is split by column into one store holding frequently accessed fields (Key, Name, Description, Price) and another holding less-used fields (Key, Stock, LastOrdered).

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of functional partitioning: a corporate data domain containing product inventory and customer tables is split into two separate databases, one for product data and one for customer data.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of the monitoring and diagnostics pipeline stages: data sources and instrumentation (application, framework, OS, infrastructure) feed collection and storage, then analysis and diagnosis (filtering, aggregation, correlation, KPI comparison), and finally visualization and alerting (dashboards, alerts, reports), with a feedback loop back to collection.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of a telemetry collection architecture: instrumentation sources (application code, infrastructure, non-Microsoft components) emit counters, events, and logs through ETW providers and an event log service into ETL files, event logs, and trace logs, which a collection service writes to storage for hot analysis and warm/cold analysis feeding visualization and alerting.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of the pull model for collecting telemetry: a monitoring agent on each of two nodes pulls ETL files, OS event logs, application trace logs, and custom trace logs locally and writes them to central shared storage.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of decoupled telemetry collection using a queue: data collection services on two nodes gather ETL files and logs, post them to a message queue, and a separate storage writing service drains the queue into shared storage.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram extending the queued telemetry collection pipeline with a separate consolidation and cleanup service that processes raw data written by the storage writing service before it lands in shared storage.

images.source: Web API and Scalability Best Practices
images.description: Diagram of partitioning consolidated monitoring data: after the storage writing and consolidation/cleanup services populate shared storage, a data partitioning service moves the data into purpose-specific stores such as Azure SQL, blob storage, and Cosmos DB.

Diagram of the Big Compute architecture style: a client submits work to a job queue handled by a scheduler/coordinator, which dispatches it either as independent parallel tasks or as tightly coupled tasks that communicate with each other.
Diagram of Azure Batch running big compute work: the Batch service manages a pool of VMs that exchange data with a storage account.
Diagram of an HPC cluster on Azure VMs: a virtual network contains cluster nodes, a cluster head node, and RDMA-networked H-series (A8-A9) nodes, all connected to a storage account.

Diagram of a hybrid HPC deployment: on-premises cluster nodes and head node connect to cluster nodes in an Azure virtual network via ExpressRoute or VPN Gateway, with the cloud nodes backed by Azure storage.

Logical component diagram of the big data architecture style: data sources flow through real-time message ingestion and stream processing on one path and batch processing on another, both feeding an analytical data store for analytics and reporting, coordinated by an orchestration component.

Reference diagram of an IoT architecture: devices connect through a field gateway to a cloud gateway, which feeds stream processing with hot path analytics, machine learning, notifications, cold storage and batch analytics, alongside a device registry, provisioning API, and command-and-control path to the application back end.
Diagram of the event-driven architecture style: event producers send events through an event ingestion component that fans them out to multiple independent event consumers.

Diagram of the N-tier architecture style: a client passes through a web application framework (WAF) to a web tier, then to two middle tiers connected by messaging, with a cache, a data tier, and a remote service.

Diagram of the Web-Queue-Worker architecture style: a client served by a CDN and identity provider hits a web front end that communicates with a worker via a queue, with both sharing a database, cache, static content, and an optional remote service.

Diagram of the microservices architecture style: clients call an API gateway in front of multiple microservices (domain services, a composition service) that communicate via publish/subscribe message-oriented middleware, each owning domain databases (SQL and NoSQL), supported by management/orchestration, observability, and DevOps capabilities.

Diagram of a physical N-tier deployment on Azure VMs: internet traffic passes through load-balanced NVAs in a perimeter network, then load balancers in front of web-tier and business-tier VM sets, ending at primary and secondary SQL Server VMs in the data tier, with DevOps access via Azure Bastion inside a virtual network.

Diagram of a Web-Queue-Worker implementation on Azure services: a client reaches a web app via Azure Content Delivery Network backed by Blob Storage, the web app passes work through a queue to a Functions app, with Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Managed Redis, and Azure SQL Database as data stores.

Diagram of Dependency Inversion: a high-level component HL1 calls through an interface <I> while the medium-level implementation ML1's source-code dependency arrow points up against the flow of control, showing polymorphism lets us choose the dependency direction.

Diagram of architectural boundaries where Business Rules define UI<I> and DB<I> interfaces that the UI and DB implement, making each side independently deployable and developable; legend distinguishes flow of control, source-code dependency direction, and the boundary.

Single Responsibility Principle violation example: an Employee class with calculatePay, reportHours, and save serves three different actors (CFO, COO, CTO), and a shared regularHours method causes accidental duplication of logic between payroll and operations.

SRP-compliant refactoring using a Facade: a thin EmployeeFacade instantiates and delegates to PayCalculator, HourReporter, and EmployeeSaver classes, which share a method-less Employee Data structure.

Alternative SRP refactoring where the Employee class keeps its data plus the most important method (calculatePay) and delegates reportHours and save to separate HourReporter and EmployeeSaver classes.

Two-panel figure of a Financial Report system: component-and-module architecture where all dependencies flow in one direction across boundaries via dependency inversion, and a hierarchy-of-protection view placing the highest-level business rules as the most protected.

Interface Segregation Principle comparison: three User classes all depending on a fat OPS class (any change forces recompiling all users) versus ISP-compliant code where each user depends only on its own segregated interface (U1Ops, U2Ops, U3Ops).

Abstract Factory pattern crossing an architectural boundary: Application calls ServiceFactory<I>.makeSvc to obtain a Service<I>, with ServiceFactoryImpl and ConcreteImpl on the concretions side; dependency lines cross the boundary only from concrete to abstract.

Tension triangle of the component cohesion principles REP, CCP, and CRP, with edge labels showing the cost of abandoning each (too many unneeded releases, too many components change, hard to reuse) and asking where your component falls in the space.

Component diagram illustrating a dependency cycle (highlighted in red) among Entities, Authorizer, and Interactors: each needs a pinned version of the next, so the components must coordinate builds and behave like a single coupled component.

Breaking a component dependency cycle with the Dependency Inversion Principle: instead of Entities' User depending directly on Authorizer's Permissions, a Permissions interface is placed inside Entities and implemented by Authorizer, reversing the dependency.

Component diagram of the system after breaking the cycle: a new Permissions component is introduced so Authorizer and Entities both depend on it, restoring an acyclic dependency graph among Main, View, Controllers, Presenters, Interactors, Database, and Entities.

Side-by-side vertical slices of two use cases, Add Order and Delete Order, each layered into UI, application-specific business rules (validations), application-independent business rules (approval or refund process), and persistence.
Diagram showing the DB and GUI components acting as plugins to the Business Rules, with boundary lines separating them and both dependency arrows pointing inward toward the business rules.

Use case example written as an index card, 'Gather Contact Info for New Loan', listing input, output, and a numbered primary course (validate name and address, get credit score, deny if below 500, else create Customer), annotated that use cases coordinate the use of entities.

The classic Clean Architecture concentric-circles diagram (Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks & Drivers) with dependencies pointing inward, plus a crossing-boundaries example where a Controller and Presenter talk to a Use Case Interactor through input and output ports.

Detailed source-code dependency diagram of a Clean Architecture scenario: Controller and Presenter communicate with a Use Case Interactor via Input/Output Data structures and Use Case ports, with a Data Access Interface shielding the database; a note stresses it shows dependencies, not flow of control.

Comparison of partial-boundary strategies: split data-access interfaces with one Users Repository implementing both (recompilation cost but boundary preserved) versus no interfaces (boundary crossed in the wrong direction, harder to split vertically later).

Partial boundary using a Facade: List All Users and List All Admin Users use cases call a Users Facade that fronts separate Users and Admin Users repositories, keeping splittable components centralized for cognitive simplicity despite the dependency crossing the boundary in the wrong direction.

Two-panel taxi aggregator case study: the architecture designed while ignoring the current microservices (Taxi Finder/Selector/Dispatcher with Rides and Parcels logic kept separate) versus its implementation in the current state of microservices, with one horizontal layer per business line and internal component boundaries.

UML use case diagram for a video streaming product with Author, Admin, Purchaser, and Viewer actors and their use cases (submit MP4, purchase licenses, view catalog, stream video), highlighting abstract use cases shared across actors with a note to keep concrete use cases separate.

Component diagram of the video streaming system partitioned by actor: Admin, Author, Purchaser, and Viewer each get Views, Presenters, Interactors, and Controllers, with Revenue/Data/Database gateways below; notes explain decoupling-mode options and that boundary crossings follow the dependency rule.

UML package diagram of a ports-and-adapters style layout marking inside versus outside: OrdersController in the web package and JdbcOrdersRepository in the database package are outside, while the domain package with OrdersService interface, OrdersServiceImpl, and Orders interface is inside.

Package-by-component diagram of an 'orders component': external code enters through a single OrdersComponent interface, package visibility modifiers hide the internals, and the well-defined component inside a monolith is presented as a steppingstone to extracting a microservice.

Side-by-side comparison of four packaging strategies for the Orders feature (package by layer, package by feature, ports and adapters, package by component); the caption notes that if every class is public the four architectures are effectively the same, differing only in folder distribution.

The same four packaging strategies (by layer, by feature, ports and adapters, by component) redrawn with Java package boundaries, using shading to distinguish public classes from package-protected ones and showing how each strategy enforces encapsulation differently.

Comparison of release flows: in a monolith, Teams A-D all feed one release candidate where any team's failure blocks production, while with microservices each team has its own independent release-to-production pipeline so only Team B's release is blocked.

Sequence-style diagram of a client device sending HTTP POST (202 Accepted) to a Scheduler service, which orchestrates HTTP GET to a User Accounts service (200 OK) and HTTP PUT to Package and Delivery services (201 Created).
Simple diagram of the repository pattern: a GetDrone() call goes to a Drone Repository which reads from a data store and returns a Drone domain entity.

Diagram of the Scheduler Service calling GET /api/drone on the Drone Service, whose internal HTTP request handler and repository fetch the Drone entity from a data store and return it serialized as JSON over the service boundary.

Two API versioning strategies side by side: a single service exposing both v1 and v2 interfaces to v1 and v2 clients, versus side-by-side deployment where separate v1 and v2 service instances each serve their matching client.
Database-per-service illustration: Service A writes to its own private data store while a red X blocks Service B from reading that store directly.

Data considerations diagram for the Drone Delivery application: Gateway, Ingestion, and Scheduler fan out to Account, 3rd Party Transport, Package, Drone, and Delivery services, with each service using its own storage technology (Cosmos DB for Package and Delivery History, Redis cache for Delivery, blob storage for history), illustrating polyglot persistence.

API gateway architecture diagram: client apps connect over TLS to an API gateway (platform or custom) that performs routing, aggregation, TLS offloading/mTLS, and response caching for Services A and B, with dotted links to an identity provider for authentication and a monitoring component for logging and metrics.

Interservice communication map of the Drone Delivery app with a legend distinguishing REST API calls (solid arrows) from events (dashed): Ingestion sends events to the Scheduler, which calls Account, 3rd Party Transport, Package, Drone, and Delivery via REST, while Delivery emits events to Delivery History and the Supervisor listens via events.

Compensating-transaction (saga) diagram: the Scheduler's calls to Account, 3rd Party Transport, and Drone succeed (OK) but the Package call fails, so a Supervisor reads from a shared message queue and sends Cancel commands to the services that had succeeded.

Azure architecture diagram of a web app in a multiple-container AKS cluster: users reach an Application Gateway routing to three nodes that host reverse proxy and Service A/B containers, all managed by an orchestrator (Azure Kubernetes Service) operated by DevOps.

Detailed container topology diagram: an API gateway routes through two reverse proxy containers to service layers for Microservices A and B, each with multiple containers (including an auto-scaled new instance, an unhealthy instance being bypassed, and a replacement healthy instance) backed by separate Azure Cosmos DB cluster databases.

Composite Azure design-patterns diagram showing a client application reaching a microservices application through Strangler Fig and an API gateway (offloading, routing, aggregation), with Backends for Frontends for desktop and mobile, a Sidecar, an event bus between services, and an Anti-corruption layer in front of a legacy system.
Four-step domain-driven design process flow: analyze domain, define bounded contexts, define entities, aggregates, and services, then identify microservices.

Hand-drawn style domain model bubble map for the drone delivery business with Shipping at the center connected to subdomains such as Drone management, Accounts, Invoicing, Returns, Video surveillance, Drone sharing, Predictive analysis, Drone repair, Third party, Call center, Loyalty, User rating, and ETA analysis.

Bounded-context map of the drone delivery domain with dashed boundary lines grouping Shipping, Drone management, Video surveillance, Drone sharing, and Accounts, while Third-party transportation and Call center are shaded and labeled as external systems.

Diagram of the Shipping bounded context containing Scheduler, Package, Delivery, and Delivery history, with the Scheduler also calling out to Accounts, Third-party transportation, and Drone management outside the context boundary.

Drone Delivery microservices design: an Ingestion service feeds a message queue consumed by the Scheduler service (watched by a Supervisor service), which calls User Account, 3rd-party transportation (external), Drone Scheduling, Package, and Delivery services, with Delivery emitting delivery events to a Delivery History service.

DDD tactical-patterns diagram showing a request flowing from an Application service through a Domain service to Aggregates — one expanded to show a root entity with a child entity and value object — and an aggregate publishing a domain event.

UML-style class box for the Delivery entity listing attributes (Id, OwnerId, Pickup and Dropoff locations, Packages REF, Expedited boolean, Confirmation, DroneId) with association multiplicities to Account (1), Package (1..*), and Drone (0..1).

Domain relationship diagram for drone delivery: a Supervisor observes the Scheduler, which coordinates the Account, Package (with Tag), Drone, and Delivery aggregates; Drone emits DroneStatus messages consumed by Delivery, which holds Confirmation and Notification and emits DeliveryStatus.

Study-plan flow chart for system design interview prep: from 'System Design Topics' choose a short, medium, or long timeline (breadth vs. depth), work through interview questions with solutions and object-oriented design questions, and review supporting material like real-world architectures and company engineering blogs.

Hand-drawn-style system design diagram of a scaled web architecture: a client resolves DNS and fetches from a CDN, while requests flow through load balancers to web servers that split into Write and Read APIs, backed by a memory cache, SQL write master-slave with read replicas, an analytics service, SQL analytics store, and an object store.

System design diagram of a Twitter-like timeline service: web servers route to Read, Write, and Search APIs, with a fan-out service feeding tweet info, user info, timeline, user graph, search, and notification services, all backed by a memory cache, SQL read replicas with a write master-slave, and an object store.

System design diagram of a web crawler / search system distinguishing user search data flow from crawler data flow: a Query API hits reverse index and document services fed through queues by a crawler service writing to NoSQL, with a memory cache for query results.

System design diagram of a Mint.com-style budgeting service: an Accounts API places tasks on a queue for a transaction extraction service that fans out to category, budget, and notification services, alongside a Read API, memory cache, SQL write master-slave with read replicas, and an object store.

System design diagram for a social-graph query service: client traffic flows through DNS, load balancers, and web servers to a Query API that calls a User Graph Service, which delegates to lookup services and person servers, with results stored in a memory cache.

System design diagram for a key-value search backend: clients reach a Query API via DNS, load balancers, and web servers; the Query API fans out to reverse index and document services and caches results in a memory cache.

System design diagram of an Amazon-style sales ranking system: web servers expose Sales and Read APIs while a Sales Rank Service computes rankings from an object store, with a CDN, memory cache, and SQL write master-slave plus read replicas completing the architecture.

System design diagram of a large-scale AWS-style architecture combining a worker service and queue with asynchronous Write APIs, a synchronous Write API and Read API, memory cache, NoSQL store, SQL write master-slave with read replicas, an object store, and SQL scaling patterns called out as sharding (customers A-M / N-Z) and federation (customers vs. products databases).
Twelve-Factor App 'build, release, run' diagram: code is transformed by a build stage and combined with config to produce a release.
Twelve-Factor App codebase diagram showing one codebase tracked in version control mapping to many deploys: production, staging, and individual developer environments.

Twelve-Factor App process-model chart plotting scale (running processes) against workload diversity (process types), showing web, worker, and clock process types scaled to different counts (e.g., four workers, two web processes, one clock).
